title: Integrated Approach for Management of Wilt of Lentil
authors: Kamlesh Ram, Ramesh Singh, A. K. Prajapati and Chandra Mani Patel
affiliations: Kamlesh Ram*1 and Ramesh Singh2, A. K. Prajapati2 and Chandra Mani Patel2
1 Deptt. of Plant Pathology, Brahmanand Post Graduate College, Rath, Hamirpur (U.P.) India
2 Deptt. of Plant Pathology, Tilak Dhari Post Graduate College Jaunpur (U.P.) India

blocks.x: Abstract:

Lentil (Lens culinaris Medikus) is a vital Rabi pulse crop in India, serving as a primary protein source for the vegetarian population. Despite its importance in food security and soil health. The primary biological constraint is lentil wilt, caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis (Fol), which can result in yield losses between the 10 to 100%. Fol is most prevalent pathogen (62.0%) associated with plant mortality, Sclerotium rolfsii & Rhizoctonia bataticola reached next. The disease is characterized by sudden seedling drooping and adult plant stunting, along with internal vascular discoloration during later stages. High soil temperatures (24–27°C) and acidic pH levels (5.2–5.8) favour pathogen growth. Early sowing in October significantly increases wilt incidence compared to late November or December plantings. Pathogen Variability, Studies across Indian states reveal significant morphological and cultural diversity among Fol isolates. The bioagent Trichoderma viride and T. harzianum demonstrate superior antagonism (up to 76.25% inhibition), Neem cake and mustard cake amendments significantly reduce soil inoculum and improve yield. Essential oils (Garlic, Thyme, Lemongrass) and plant extracts (Eucalyptus, Neem) serve as effective "green fungicides". Seed treatments with carbendazim, tebuconazole, and carboxin provide maximum inhibition of mycelial growth. Sustainable lentil production requires an integrated disease management approach. Combining resistant genotypes with optimized sowing dates, bio-priming with Trichoderma, and organic soil amendments offers the most robust defense against Fusarium wilt, ensuring both crop profitability and environmental safety.
Keywords: Lentil, Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, Bioagent, Bioactive compounds & fungicides.
Introduction:

India is one of the major pulses (Legumes) producing countries in the world. Pulses form an important ingredient of Indian diet as they contribute to major protein supplement to feed the majority of Indian vegetarian population, which cannot afford animal protein being too expensive. Pulse production in the country remained almost stagnant, thereby causing a considerable worry in the minds of all those concerned. While the importance of pulses in daily diet is so well established, there has not been any significant breakthrough in pulse production in the country as it fluctuates between 11 to 12 million tons, leading to an unfavorable demand and supply position causing in sharp rise in the prices of pulses. Thus, the per capita availability of pulses is far below, the WHO recommendation dose. Additionally, pest and diseases contribute significantly to the losses in yield, hence is an unequivocal need to manage pulse diseases. Lentil (Lens culinaris Medikus) was among the first crops domesticated and has become an important food legume crop in the farming and food systems of many countries globally. The seeds that are a rich source of protein, minerals, and vitamins needed for the humans health and straw byproduct is a useful animal feed. Its ability in nitrogen and carbon sequestration improves soil nutrient status, which in turn provides sustainability in production systems Sarker and Erskine (2006). It is a Rabi pulse crop that is sown from October to November. The productivity of lentils in India is 1023 kg/ha (AICRP 2024), which is also lower than the global average of 1245.5 kg/ha (FAOSTAT 2023). This may be the result of inappropriate agricultural practices and crop management strategies.
The economic significance and distribution of lentil wilt:

In India, farmer’s tendencies to grow lentil in fields where other crops do not perform well, primarily under rain-fed conditions, where the crop suffers substantial damage due to several illnesses in addition to water stress, are the main restrictions responsible for low lentil yields in India. Lentil disease is caused by a variety of fungus, viruses, and nematodes. Ascochyta blight, rust, wilt, root rot complex, collar rot and downy mildew are some of the more commonly observed and possibly damaging ones Agrawal and Prasad (1997). Infections with lentils not only reduce yield but also deteriorate seed quality. Chaudhary, et al. (2010) reported the first time a national lentil wilt-root rot incidence at the crucial reproductive stage and their associated pathogens. The main pathogens found associated with plant mortality at this stage were 62.0% Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, 25.2% Rhizoctonia bataticola and 9.8% Sclerotium rolfsii. Choudhary and Kumar (2016) Fusarium wilt has been reported to cause 100% yield losses, if it affects the crop in the seedling stage. Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, the severe causative agent of lentil wilt has been appearing in severe form for long time and causing a major problem in lentil growing part of the country. Stoilova and Chavdarov (2006) found that lentil is the second pulse crop after dry bean in Bulgaria. Lentil wilt and Ascochyta blight are two diseases that significantly lower lentil output. Three of the examined accessions (91-001, 91-028, and 98-001) were sensitive to Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, accounting for 45 and 50% of the total wilted plant, out of 32 lentil genotypes with varying geographical origins. Taylor, et al. (2007) reported that lentil, fungus infections are the most significant biological limitation to production. The major fungal infections that can cause serious losses in most lentil-growing regions of the world are Ascochyta lentis and Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis. Lentil plants are susceptible to a wide range of bacterial and fungal diseases. Bean leaf roll virus, beet western yellows virus, or subterranean clover red leaf virus produce lentil yellows disease, which is found all over the world. Integrated disease management techniques, including as the use of resistant cultivars, changed cultural methods, and the application of fungicides or insecticides, can help to minimize the spread of disease.

Chen, et al. (2009) reported that lentil is an important crop in many parts of the world, cultivated under various production systems. Lentil crops are affected by a number of diseases caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses and nematodes. Some diseases are common in most lentil-growing regions worldwide, whereas others are limited to certain production areas. Proper management of these diseases is necessary to ensure sustainable productivity and profitability of lentil.

Chaudhary, et al. (2009) reported that lentil is the second most important Rabi pulse crop of India and suffers heavy plant mortality due to wilt, root rot and collar rot at different stages of crop growth. Many root-invading diseases favor crop invasion due to congenial soil temperature and moisture during early crop growth, winter rains, and terminal dryness. The current study, which included 265 samples from 76 districts across seven Indian states, found that 12 distinct fungi were involved, with Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis having the strongest correlation.

Lodhi, et al. (2016) reported that yield losses due to this disease vary from 10 to 100% depending upon the climatic conditions and susceptibility of the host plant. It grows best at a temperature of 25 °C and a pH of 5–6.5. It results in drooping leaves, brown to black discolouration, and young seedling death, among other symptoms. Both soil-borne and seed-borne fungi are possible.

Yield Loss: Lentil wilt acts as a major constraint on productivity, with severe, often, causing complete crop failure. Studies have recorded varying disease incidences (6.62%–20.36%) in Madhya Pradesh, with some reports showing higher incidences in susceptible varieties Kharte, at el. (2023).
Symptomatology:

Seedling stage: - In the second fortnight of November, two to three weeks after seeding, the disease's symptoms were noticed on the seedling. The symptoms characterized by browning of radical, stunting, sudden drooping and drying of leaves and finally collapse of seedling. The root are healthy but having reduce spreading, nodulation and do not show internal discoloration of the vascular system. Adult stages: The affected plant showed typical wilting, which may occur in the field up to flowering and pod filling stage. The initial symptom is appearing in isolated patches. The growths of infected plants are stunted, curling from lower to upper parts of the plant and there leaves dull green to turn gradually all leaves yellow and straw colored. The crown droops and ultimately the whole plant or in the individual branches are death. The roots of the affected plant gradually turn yellowish brown to dark brown partial or complete. The roots nodules are poorly developed.

Garkoti, et al. (2013) reported that at both seedling and adult stages, the disease shows in patches throughout the field. Seedling wilt manifests itself as sudden drooping, followed by leaf drying and seedling death. The roots appear to be in good health, with little or no nodulation and no internal vascular system discoloration. Adult wilt symptoms arise between the blooming and late pod-filling stages and are characterized by sudden drooping of the infected plant's top leaflets, leaflet closure without premature shedding, dull green leaves, and wilting of the entire plant or individual branches. Seeds from plants that have been impacted between mid-pod-fill and late pod-fill are frequently shriveled.
Isolation and culture Media:

Jalander and Gachande (2015.) also found that Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. udum isolated from seven different varieties of pigeon pea using Czapek's dox agar, potato dextrose agar and glucose nitrate agar. The colonies grown on CDA and GNA were showed maximum fluffy growth; on PDA it was appressed in a similar manner. Pathogen mycelial color and substrate color differ on different media.

Joseph, et al. (2017) the effects of mycological media and temperature on mycelial growth and spore production of three fungal pathogens recently reported on Ricinodendron heudelotii were investigated. The pathogens were identified as Pestalotiopsis microspora, Lasiodiplodia theobromae and Fusarium oxysporum. The growth rate and conidia concentration of the fungi was assessed on three culture media: potato dextrose agar, malt extract agar and V8 juice agar.

Kumar, et al. (2019) Fusarium verticillioides grew best on PDA and Richard's agar media among seven culture media tested. The most suitable pH level for growth of fungus was 6.0 and 6.5 with excellent sporulation. Growth of the fungus was maximum at 27 ℃ after seven days of inoculation, which was reduced drastically below 18 ℃ and above 30 ℃.
Pathogenicity Test:

In Northwestern Algeria, wilted lentil plants yielded thirty-two isolates of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis. Mutual heterokaryon-forming isolates were assigned to the same vegetative compatibility group (VCG). The Fol isolates represented a single race but differed in their aggressiveness on susceptible lines. According to Belabid and Fortas (2002), Nit-1 mutations were the most common (63%), followed by Nit-M (31%) and Nit-3 (6%).

Pouralibaba (2005) reported that13 isolates from different parts of Iran add another from Syria. were manipulated in some experiments to identify contingent pathogenic variation among population of lentil wilt pathogen agent (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis) The results showed different growth speed pattern between isolates on the cultures which had been measured as diameter of colony after seven days. These results confirmed that differences among the fungus population totally are related to different aggressiveness properties and not virulence patterns.

Taheri, et al. (2010) Pathogenic and genetic characterization of thirty three isolates of Fusarium oxysporum were obtained from wilted lentil plants collected from different lentil growing areas in Northern and Razavi Khorasan provinces. Pathogenicity tests were performed for all isolates on the susceptible lines. Results indicated that 27 isolates were pathogenic. Each isolate's genetic similarity was determined using the Dice similarity coefficient, and a dendrogram illustrating their link was created using cluster analysis. Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis was isolated from wilted lentis plants that were gathered from various lentis growing regions in Iran, according to Mohammadi et al. (2011). Every isolate underwent a pathogenicity test. According to analysis, Fol isolates could be divided into three groups using the Bayaa scales. Six primers were used in the ISSR approach to assess the amount of genetic variation, and each primer was able to demonstrate the variety among isolates. The findings demonstrated that the aggressiveness of the Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis isolates varies on the susceptible lines. Primers (CAG) 5 and ISSR10 showed the highest diversity (93%), whereas SR02 showed the lowest diversity (50%).
Growth habits and Culture characters:

Thirty-two isolates of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis (Fol) were gathered from several lentil-growing regions in Northwest Algeria, according to Belabid et al. (2004). Using a set of six RAPD primers and three AFLP selective nucleotide primer pairs, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification was used to assess the amount of genetic variation in the study. The findings showed that while the Fol isolates are representative of a single race, their levels of aggression on the susceptible lines vary. The Jaccard similarity coefficient was used to determine the genetic similarity between each isolate, and a dendrogram was produced using cluster analysis.

Datta, et al. (2009) observed that twenty four isolates of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis (Fol,) collected from different lentil growing areas of the Gangetic plain showed variation with respect to cultural and morphological characters. A set of 40 RAPD primers and 12 SSR primer pairs were used to assess the degree of genetic diversity. Based on RAPD and SSR markers, the results show that a subpopulation of Fol had minimal genetic variability.

The variations in cultural and morphological characters (isolates Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa & West Bengal) on Potato Dextrose Agar medium. The colony diameter ranged from 29.6 to 57.3 mm after eight days of incubation at 27±2 ℃. Six isolates produced white mycelia color, serrated margin with fluffy growth with light and dark yellow pigmentation while four isolates produced partially appressed growth with dark yellow to brown pigmentation in substrate. The dry mycelium weight ranged from 98.3 to 201.0 mg, from Potato Dextrose broth medium after 15 days at 27±2 ℃. The size of macro conidia and micro conidia ranged from 15.4 - 45.0 × 2.1 - 6.2 µm and 2.5-17.5×2.1-6.2 µm, respectively. Pathogenic variability on soil inoculated pot grown plants of pigeonpea resulted in 0.0 to 42.3 percent wilt incidence, observed by Kumar and Upadhyay (2014).

Altaf, et al. (2014) noticed 15 isolates of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis were observed. The length and width of micro-conidia of these isolates ranged from 4.38 to 6.65 µm and 2.31 to 3.2 µm, respectively. The mean diameter of chlamydospores ranged from 7.0 to 15.8 µm. This line proved to be more resistant than Masoor-93.

Wilt is one of the most significant lentil diseases, according to Hiremani and Dubey (2016), and it is brought on by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis. The pathogen's physical traits and aggressiveness were assessed in 75 isolates from seven distinct lentil-growing states in India. The color of the colonies ranged from white to purple, with white being the most prevalent for 40 isolates. On the sensitive cultivar Sehore 74-3, the isolates' aggressiveness varied greatly, resulting in wilt incidence ranging from 20 to 80%. Patra and Biswas (2017) studied the eleven isolates of Fusarium oxysporum f. ciceri were studied for its cultural, morphological and pathogenic variability. Radial growth of isolates ranged from 72 mm to 87 mm at seven days after inoculation on PDA medium. The size of macro-conidia was ranged from 13-15 x 2-3 µm to 15-19 x 3-4 µm in micro conidia was form 3-4 x 1-2 µm to 5-6 x 2-3 µm. Shape of most macro conidia is sickle and micro conidia are round to oval shaped. Most of the isolates were highly pathogenic. Five isolates of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. ricini from various castor-growing regions of Gujarat were examined for their cultural and morphological diversity. Each isolate exhibited significant variation in cultural characteristics, mycelial colour, pigmentation, sporulation, size of micro-conidia and macro-conidia. Rose Bengal medium, Potato dextrose medium, Richard's medium, Asthana and Hawker's medium and Glucose asparagine medium were used to study the fungi. Findings will be useful for developing Fusarium wilt resistant castor hybrids/varieties observed by Sangava, et al. (2018).

Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis has been found to be one of the main dangers to lentil agriculture in India, causing vascular wilt of lentils. The isolates from this colony of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis were white, dull white, pinkish white, yellowish white, and brownish white. On a typical Hi-media Potato Dextrose Agar medium, the pigmentations were dark tan, creamy, dark brown, and yellowish brown. Based on the size of the macroconidia, which were defined as larger than 15 µm, the pace of mycelia growth was divided into three groups. Because isolates from different states were mixed together, the heterogeneity in F. oxysporum f. sp. lentis isolates was not restricted by state lines. The phylogenetic tree that was created took into account the isolates' various physical and cultural traits. (2018) Saxena et al.
Role of environment factors on severity of the disease:

The role of soil pH and atmospheric temperature on lentil wilt development has been studied for the first time in a controlled experiment. The pathogen Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis favored a pH range of 5.2-5.8, and an optimum temperature range was 24-27 ℃ Kaushal and Sharma (1999). Hwang, et al. (2000) reported that root rot symptoms were most severe at warm temperatures (20 to 27.5 °C) and declined in warmer or cooler soils. F. avenaceum inoculation decreased seed production and establishment.

Pusa 212' and 'BGD 1005' chickpea cultivars were tested for influence of environmental parameters on wilt caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. ciceris. Lowest mean wilt incidence (22.6–25.5%) and maximum mean grain yield (13.5–14.3 tonnes / ha) were recorded in the crop sown on 10 and 20 November. Maximum and minimum ambient temperature and soil temperature were positively and significantly correlated with wilt incidence in Pusa 212 (Mina and Dubey 2010).

Garkoti, et al. (2013) Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis is soil borne and can survive in the soil and plant debris for a period of 3-4 years. The disease is favoured by low soil temperature, 30% soil water holding capacity and increasing plant maturity. Yield losses depend on the stage at which the plant wilts - it can be 100% when wilt occurs at pre pod stage or 67% when it occurs at the pre harvest stage. Studied effect of temperature and sowing time against lentil wilt caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis. Increased amount of inoculum resulted higher number of diseased plants. However, increased inoculum proved to be ineffective under cooler conditions. Early sowing associated with high soil temperature (22.6 °C) rendered maximum wilt incidence (97.2%). This report suggests development of late sown variety could be a good option to suppress this disease by Ghatak, et al. (2015).

Environmental factors a significant influence the development of lentil wilt incidence caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis. The maximum disease incidence (28.33%) was observed in the 22 October during 2019 crop season, when the average temperature and average relative humidity was 23.45°C and 67.5 per cent respectively. The minimum disease incidence 4.50% recorded on 24 December 2019 and 6.20% in the year of 24 December 2018 in respect to average temperature 10.05 and 13.35°C and relative humidity 85.5 and 73.5 percent respectively Ram and Singh(2021a).
Management
Use of different plant oils:

Belabid, et al. (2010) Fusarium lentil wilt is an important disease and is considered as a limiting factor to lentil production in Algeria. The use of the plant extracts is recently advocated by several researches, as a potential control method of plant diseases. Results obtained showed that the treatments 10 and 5% with the powders of Inula viscosa and Mentha pepirita and the essential oils formulation in all treatments significantly reduced the soil population densities of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis.

According to Charles et al. (2016), essential oils had the strongest antifungal activity, followed by cold water and ethanol extracts. The essential oils of Callistemon citrinus, Cymbopogon citratus, and Ocimum gratissimum were the most effective in preventing Phytophtora infestans from growing entirely radially and germinating conidia. The results could help create new green fungicides to prevent Fusarium wilt and late blight in tomatoes.

Singh, et al. (2017) evaluated among the botanicals, Neem oil formulation (Nemazal) and Garlic oil exhibited significant effect on the test fungus. The rate of sporulation of Fusarium oxysporum (wilt of chilli) decreased linearly with an increase in concentration and the type of botanical used. Garlic oil was highly effective (100%) even at 5 per cent concentration, whereas, Neem oil was comparatively less effective (59.63%). Similarly, rests of the leaf extracts were statistically at par to mustard oil (93.75%), Datura (90.94%), Withania somnifera (87.50%) and Chrysanthemum (30.37%).

The ability of essential oils from different aromatic plants to induce systemic resistance in chickpea seedlings and biocontrol Fusarium wilt. The antifungal activity of essential oils against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. ciceris (FOC) and their impact on the development of systemic resistance in chickpeas were assessed in this study. The main components of thyme, lemongrass, and laurel essential oils were carvacrol, geraniol, and 1,8-cineole. These oils were highly successful in lessening the severity of FOC-induced chickpea infections, according to in vitro testing. Their respective inhibition rates were 99.3 and 88.9%. The buildup of phenolic chemicals is the main cause of chickpea resistance. Thyme has the highest polyphenol content (22.7 to 57.5 mg/g) (Moutassem et al. 2019).
Use of plant extracts:

In vitro research was used to assess the antifungal properties of crude medicinal plant extracts from 20 different plant species. All plant extracts at 50% concentration were effective in reducing the mycelial growth of Fusarium oxysporum. Among the 20 plant extracts, in different solvents, higher inhibition was noticed in 4 plants extracts namely Adhatoda vasica, Jatropha curcas, Sapindus emarginatus and Vitex negundo. In-Vitro pot culture experiments showed an increase in the root and shoot length and fresh and dry weight of six plant species observed by Siva, et al. (2008).

Garlic, neem, eucalyptus, tulsi, and other plant extracts can reduce the losses caused by Fusarium wilt. The use of synthetic fungicides has resulted in a number of issues, including environmental contamination, residual effects in grains, and the killing of non-target organisms. Maximum per cent disease reduction was found in Eucalysptus (25.50%) and Garlic (28.00%) at 10% concentration of 60 days after sowing, observed by Chandra, et al. (2018).
Use of bio-agents:

Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis is one of the most important factors of reducing lentil yield in the world. Effect of four soil borne fungi on lentil wilt was evaluated in a completely randomized design under greenhouse condition. Pathogen was inoculated to soil pots three times (10 days before sowing, while sowing and 10 days after sowing) Different growth factors namely: plant heights, root length, dry weight of shoot and root and disease severity were assessed in flowering stage. Results revealed that the most effect of combination of antagonistic fungi was observed in pots inoculated with treatment (S. vermifera + T. harzianum) Dolatabadi and Goltapeh (2010).

The potential of bio-agents against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis. In this research work nineteen isolates of Trichoderma were isolated and these were described to three species. The isolate Th-5 was found to be more efficient amongst all, as they showed better antagonism against the tested phytopathogen. Efficacies of these bio-antagonists were investigated In - Vitro conditions by employing dual culture technique and liquid culture filtrate assays evaluated by Choudhary and Mohankain (2012).

According to Dolatabadi et al. (2012), Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis causes lentil wilt. One of the primary obstacles to good lentil cultivation is sp. lentis. Four antagonistic fungi—Piriformospora indica, Sebacina vermifera, Trichoderma viride, and Trichoderm harzianum—as well as their combinations were assessed for their ability to prevent this illness. At the flowering stage, the following parameters were measured: plant height, plant dry weight, root length, root dry weight, and disease severity. Two pathogen isolates were implanted in pot culture trials at three different times: prior to, concurrently with, and following sowing. Pots treated with S. vermifera + T. harzianum showed the highest plant height and the lowest disease severity for the two pathogen isolates.

Akter, et al. (2018) Assessment of antagonism of T. harzianum against F. oxysporum by In-Vitro and ex-Vitro to reduce lentil wilt was the goal of this study. According to an In Vitro investigation, T. harzianum IMI 392432 inhibited the growth of F. oxysporum most in both dual culture methods, although the inhibition was greatest (mean PIRG-73%) in technique -2. 100%. The culture filtrate included Trichoderma metabolites. The growth of pathogens is completely stopped by the PDA media. of an ex-vitro pot research, lentil plants treated with tricho-compost shown the greatest reduction of the incidence of wilt and other combinations. Wilt disease was most common (63%) when standard compost and Fusarium spore solution were used together. Kumari and Ashraf (2019) Evaluated the efficacy of 8 different bio-agents In-Vitro Viz; T. harzianum, T. viride, T. koningii, T. atroviride, T. virens, T. asperellum, T. hamatum, and Pseudomonas fluorescens, used against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis. The germination percentage, plumule length, radical length, and general vigor of lentils are all enhanced by these bioagents. T. harzianum had the highest seedling vigor index (1073.29) of the biocontrol agents. T. atroviride, however, had the lowest seedling vigor index (579.54). Prasad, et al. (2019) tested the bio-agents (Trichoderma viride, T. harzianum and Pseudomonas fluorescence) produce toxic volatile metavolatile, which reduced the radial growth of the test fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. baisilici).

Kumar, et al. (2021) tested five antagonists’ In Vitro condition against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, causing wilt of lentil. Out of all the bio-agents examined, Trichoderma viride (76.25%) was the most effective, followed by Chaetomium globosum (75.00%) and Pseudomonas fluorescens (71.25%). Namdev, et al. (2025) In the present study suggests bio-control potential of three Trichoderma strains in four cultivated and nine new genotypes of lentil. T. viride exhibited maximum 67.57 per cent inhibition of F. oxysporum f. sp. lentis, (FOL) followed by T. harzianum strain-2 (65.48%) in dual culture assay. In field conditions, T. harzianum strain 1 displayed the maximum effectiveness, showing the minimum average wilt incidence 16.37 %, followed by T. harzianum strain-2 (19.28%) as compared to the control (35.18%).
Date of sowing:

Early spring to early winter sowing dates can limit the ultimate amount of disease, delay the onset of Fusarium wilt epidemics, and slow their development. The susceptibility of the chickpea cultivar as well as the virulence and inoculum density of the Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. ciceris race may also have an impact on the overall outcome of this disease control strategy, albeit to a lesser degree (Navas-Cortes, et al. 1998). Sallam, and Abdel-Monaim (2012) recorded that some agricultural practices on suppression of lentil wilt disease. The highest average of wilt plants was occurred at the sowing date 1st October (16.4 and 14.5% wilt) in both tested seasons, respectively. On the other hand, planting at 1st December recorded the lowest wilt (14.5%) in both seasons. Highest seed yield was recorded when lentil seeds were sowed on 1st November - producing 461.2 and 499.3 kg fed.-1.
Use of Organic amendment:

Evaluated that Neem cake extract showed the highest inhibitory effect on Fusarium solani of all eleven extracts tested by poisoned food technique, followed by Mustard cake (77.77%) and Sesamum cake (63.88%), Poultry manure (55.55%), Vermicompost (49.72%) and Pressmud (49.72%) Patel, et al. (2014). Ghante, et al. (2019) studied the efficacy of soil amendment against Fusarium wilt. Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. udum is one of the most devastating soil-borne diseases causing wilt of pigeonpea. The aim of this study was to evaluate the antifungal activities of soil amendments and elicitors in pot culture. Compost, Vermicompost, Poultry manure, Sheep manure, Groundnut cake, Soybean seed cake, Castor cake, and Mustard cake significantly reduced mortality except Gypsum and Safflower seed cake. Maximum reduction of wilt incidence over control was recorded in Neem seed cake followed by Castor seed cake (66.66%). Kumari, et al. (2020) observed In-Vitro condition, among organic amendments, maximum disease control (42.02 per cent), minimum average disease incidence (36.33 per cent) and minimum pathogen spores were observed in neem cake amendment followed by poultry manure and vermicompost. This suggests that Fusarium wilt disease can be successfully managed in Rajasthan using organic farming practices. Ram and Singh (2022) evaluated seven soil amendments such as Pyrite and Gypsum @ 2.0 gm/kg soil and Neem cake, Mustard cake, Paddy straw and Wheat straw @ 20.0 gm/kg against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, causing wilt of lentil. Neem cake @ 20.0 gm/kg soil was found significantly superior over all the treatments resulting minimum wilt disease incidence (34.80 and 35.90%) maximum disease reduction over control (57.24 and 56.25%) maximum yield (6.30 and 6.50 q/ha.) and maximum yield increase over control (186.36 and 242.10%) in the years 2018-19 and 2019-20 respectively.
Use of different Chemicals:

Singh, et al. (2010) evaluated six fungicides In-Vitro and In-Vivo, against Fusarium oxysporum f sp. lentis revealed that Carbendazim and Carboxin completely inhibited the growth of test pathogen, while Thiram and Captafol inhibited 87.5 and 83.1% of mycelial growth, respectively. Seed treatment with these chemicals improved seed germination (90.0 & 89.0), root length (10.1 cm & 10.0 cm) and shoot length (4.8 cm. & 4.8cm) as compared to rest of the fungicides. Foliar spray with two fungicides separately gave the best results in reducing the wilt incidence from 37.5 to 5.0% in both the cases.

Kumar and Tripathi (2012) tested in the field against lentil wilt, it was found that seed treatment with Bayleton showed the significant response with respect to the disease incidence, 1000 grian weight (g) and yield (kg/ha) followed by Mancozeb and Captafol. Additionally, it was noted that seed treatment with Bayleton (2 g/kg seed) produced the highest grain production and the lowest disease incidence compared to other treatments.

Six fungicides were tested in vitro against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense by Somu et al. (2014). At concentrations of 500, 1000, and 2000 ppm, carbendazim, carboxin, propiconazole, and benomyl completely inhibited the fungal growth. On the other hand, at a dosage of 2000 ppm, Difenconazole completely inhibited the growth of the fungus.

The effectiveness of bioagents, botanicals, and seed dresser fungicides against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis in vivo. The highest per cent disease control was found in T8 Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% + Neem leaf extract + P. fluorescens (87.75%) followed by T6, T7, T8 and T9. as compared to T9 control (0.0) by Chandra, et al. (2020).

Eight fungicides were investigated in vitro by Kumar et al. (2021) against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, which causes lentil wilt. Carbendazim 50%WP, Cymoxanil 8%+ Mancozeb 64%, Tebuconazole 25.9% EC, and Propiconazol 25% EC were reported to completely block the pathogen's mycelial development at all three concentrations (50 ppm, 75 ppm, and 100 ppm).

Ram and Singh (2021) evaluated seven fungicides In-Vitro against Fusarium oxysporum f sp. lentis revealed that Carbendazim completely inhibited the growth of test pathogen, while Benomyl, Topsin-M, Ridomil and Vitavax were found next best in inhibited mycelial growth of the pathogen up to 92.11% to 83.46% respectively.
Conclusion:

The lentil crop has been facing numerous plant diseases, in the absence of any control measure and reduces the plant growth, seed quality and yield. In the region where lentils are grown, lentil wilt, which is caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis, is the most severe and ineffective disease. In India and other nations where lentils are grown, a survey was conducted to gauge the severity of lentil wilt. The severity of the wilt varied from location to location. The seedling and pod formation stages are when the symptoms first arise. Colony pigments and physical traits vary between the isolates. It is possible to manage wilt using a variety of integrated approaches, including plant oils, plant extracts, bio-agents, and dates of sowing, organic amendments, and various fungicides used to minimize the losses. This study provides information about the epidemiology of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis that helps various species of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis and encourages the cultivation of new varieties for the management of wilt incidence and increased production.
